{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"# Choice screens are not market choice.

A choice screen looks like competition: several services, one prompt, your finger poised over a neat stack of logos. But the first question isn’t which option you’ll pick. It’s who decided which options could appear at all (and which rivals vanished before the screen was drawn). If one firm writes the guest list, orders the seats, and keeps the door, are you choosing a market or choosing inside its lobby? We should call the screen what it is: an interface designed by a gatekeeper.

The selector controls more than admission. It can set eligibility rules, charge for placement, exclude software that conflicts with its business, or require every candidate to use infrastructure it owns. Even an apparently neutral rule can favor incumbents – a requirement that’s cheap for a giant may be ruinous for a small developer. You see five choices, but you don’t see the fifty services that couldn’t satisfy rules written by their largest competitor. The visible menu is merely the last stage of selection.

Then comes the default. Defaults aren’t suggestions floating weightlessly beside equal alternatives. They benefit from haste, familiarity, setup fatigue, and the reasonable assumption that the device maker chose something that works. Your users have jobs to finish; they didn’t buy a phone or install an operating system to conduct a procurement exercise. Put one service first, preselect it, give it a smoother sign-in, and make switching require six extra taps (a quiet little obstacle course), and nominal equality becomes behavioral inequality.

Developers know this pattern because we build it. A default is code with a distribution strategy attached. It determines which API receives the first request, which account gathers the first history, and which product acquires the data that improves its next offer. Once your contacts, purchases, preferences, or files accumulate there, switching gets harder. The default wins twice – first by placement, then by converting placement into dependence.

The gatekeeper’s defense is predictable: “Every user can choose.” That claim describes a button, not a market. I don’t care whether an alternative is technically reachable if the gatekeeper still chooses the candidates, ranks them, designs the prompt, and controls the path back later. That’s like letting a casino deal the cards, mark the deck, and then boasting that every player freely chose a seat. The freedom is real in the thinnest possible sense; the power remains where it started.

Of course, a choice screen can help. I’d rather have a clear prompt than an invisible default, and a short list may spare people an absurd setup ritual. But the remedy fails when it leaves the gatekeeper in charge of every upstream condition. A screen can redistribute some clicks while preserving control over interoperability, installation, payments, data portability, and access to users. Calling that “competition” is bullshit dressed in radio buttons (the interface supplies the costume).

My test is simple: can a rival reach you without begging its competitor for admission, and can you leave one service without abandoning the value you created there? A meaningful remedy changes those conditions. It establishes transparent eligibility rules, bars self-preferencing, permits independent installation, and makes defaults easy to change. It also requires practical portability and interoperable paths where those are technically feasible (with security rules aimed at actual risks rather than commercial inconvenience).

Enforcement matters too. The gatekeeper shouldn’t be allowed to rewrite the rules whenever a rival gains ground, or bury switching behind warnings that make ordinary choice feel reckless. We need audits, complaint procedures, penalties that exceed the profit from obstruction, and remedies that can evolve when evasion does. Otherwise the screen becomes regulatory theater – a compliance layer sitting atop the same machinery.

Market choice begins before your finger reaches the screen. It begins with who may build, how software reaches users, whether switching carries your work with you, and whether the platform can punish a successful rival. We can keep the prompt, but we shouldn’t confuse the menu with the market. Choice screens display options; meaningful choice changes who has the power to supply them.","omitted":[],"refused":""}

# Choice screens are not market choice.

A choice screen looks like competition: several services, one prompt, your finger poised over a neat stack of logos. But the first question isn’t which option you’ll pick. It’s who decided which options could appear at all (and which rivals vanished before the screen was drawn). If one firm writes the guest list, orders the seats, and keeps the door, are you choosing a market or choosing inside its lobby? We should call the screen what it is: an interface designed by a gatekeeper.

The selector controls more than admission. It can set eligibility rules, charge for placement, exclude software that conflicts with its business, or require every candidate to use infrastructure it owns. Even an apparently neutral rule can favor incumbents – a requirement that’s cheap for a giant may be ruinous for a small developer. You see five choices, but you don’t see the fifty services that couldn’t satisfy rules written by their largest competitor. The visible menu is merely the last stage of selection.

Then comes the default. Defaults aren’t suggestions floating weightlessly beside equal alternatives. They benefit from haste, familiarity, setup fatigue, and the reasonable assumption that the device maker chose something that works. Your users have jobs to finish; they didn’t buy a phone or install an operating system to conduct a procurement exercise. Put one service first, preselect it, give it a smoother sign-in, and make switching require six extra taps (a quiet little obstacle course), and nominal equality becomes behavioral inequality.

Developers know this pattern because we build it. A default is code with a distribution strategy attached. It determines which API receives the first request, which account gathers the first history, and which product acquires the data that improves its next offer. Once your contacts, purchases, preferences, or files accumulate there, switching gets harder. The default wins twice – first by placement, then by converting placement into dependence.

The gatekeeper’s defense is predictable: “Every user can choose.” That claim describes a button, not a market. I don’t care whether an alternative is technically reachable if the gatekeeper still chooses the candidates, ranks them, designs the prompt, and controls the path back later. That’s like letting a casino deal the cards, mark the deck, and then boasting that every player freely chose a seat. The freedom is real in the thinnest possible sense; the power remains where it started.

Of course, a choice screen can help. I’d rather have a clear prompt than an invisible default, and a short list may spare people an absurd setup ritual. But the remedy fails when it leaves the gatekeeper in charge of every upstream condition. A screen can redistribute some clicks while preserving control over interoperability, installation, payments, data portability, and access to users. Calling that “competition” is bullshit dressed in radio buttons (the interface supplies the costume).

My test is simple: can a rival reach you without begging its competitor for admission, and can you leave one service without abandoning the value you created there? A meaningful remedy changes those conditions. It establishes transparent eligibility rules, bars self-preferencing, permits independent installation, and makes defaults easy to change. It also requires practical portability and interoperable paths where those are technically feasible (with security rules aimed at actual risks rather than commercial inconvenience).

Enforcement matters too. The gatekeeper shouldn’t be allowed to rewrite the rules whenever a rival gains ground, or bury switching behind warnings that make ordinary choice feel reckless. We need audits, complaint procedures, penalties that exceed the profit from obstruction, and remedies that can evolve when evasion does. Otherwise the screen becomes regulatory theater – a compliance layer sitting atop the same machinery.

Market choice begins before your finger reaches the screen. It begins with who may build, how software reaches users, whether switching carries your work with you, and whether the platform can punish a successful rival. We can keep the prompt, but we shouldn’t confuse the menu with the market. Choice screens display options; meaningful choice changes who has the power to supply them.
